Community spotlight

News story: Community lifts families during deployment

Program Director Chris Cox sat down with local news to share how partners step in when Guard families face deployments. The feature highlights a free horse camp hosted by Jester Park Equestrian Center that gave military youth room to breathe, laugh, and stay connected while a parent was away.

  • Why it mattered: Volunteers, donors, and Jester Park covered every cost so Guard kids could simply show up.
  • What families said: Time with the horses eased anxiety and sparked conversations about deployment in a safe setting.
  • How to use it: Share this clip with civic groups and potential sponsors who want real examples of community impact.

Full interview: Chris Cox explains how community partners like Jester Park Equestrian Center rally around Guard families to keep kids grounded during deployment.

Parent perspective

Finding friendship after a cross-country move

When one Guard family relocated from Texas to Iowa, their daughter wondered who would understand what military life felt like. In this short clip, her mom shares how a familiar face from an Iowa CYP program turned into instant camaraderie—and how that connection steadied their whole household.

  • Shared experience: A fellow military youth spotted her at camp and reminded her she wasn’t starting over alone.
  • Ripple effect: Confidence followed her home, making the new duty station feel less overwhelming.
  • Takeaway: CYP friendships can outlast moves and mobilizations, giving kids anchors no matter the zip code.

Use this testimony when talking with school counselors, partner organizations, or potential sponsors who want to understand the on-the-ground impact of CYP relationships.

Altoona Teen Honored for Service to Iowa Guard Families

Johnston, Iowa | April 15, 2023

Published April 29, 2023

Life as a military child comes with challenges that are often unseen. For Klaryssa “Klair” Dunwoody, those challenges became an invitation to lead. The Altoona teen and daughter of Iowa Army National Guard Capt. Josh Dunwoody was awarded the 2023 Iowa Army National Guard Youth Volunteer Award for her dedication to Guard Soldiers and families.

“Life as a military kid isn’t always the easiest,” said Capt. Dunwoody. “But you can either survive it or you can decide to thrive in it.” Klair chose to thrive by showing up for other Guard youth.

Finding Her Place Through Service
Three years ago Klair joined the State Teen Panel (STP). The team tripled in size and expanded its role in shaping Guard family events statewide. Teen leaders plan, set up, and run events like Trunk or Treat, Cookies with Santa, and helped launch the first Military Family Ball. “It’s like a different kind of family,” she said.

Serving Families, Supporting Soldiers
Beyond STP duties, Klair volunteers at deployment events, often providing childcare so service members can attend briefings. Her presence lowers stress for parents and younger military kids navigating Guard life.

Recognition and Looking Ahead
Klair was nominated for Army Military Child of the Year in 2022 and selected as Iowa’s semifinalist; she was nominated again in 2023. For her family, the real impact is the relationships built along the way — proof that youth leadership strengthens the Guard community.

The Iowa National Guard Child & Youth Program continues to provide opportunities like the State Teen Panel to connect, empower, and support military youth across the state.

Iowa Teen Steps Into Statewide Leadership Role as GTP Representative

Johnston, Iowa | December 15, 2025

Published January 28, 2026

For many military teens, leadership begins quietly — by showing up, listening, and choosing to serve. For Charlee Cromwell, that steady commitment has led to a new statewide leadership role supporting Guard youth across Iowa and the greater Region 7 area.

Charlee, a military-connected teen from Perry, Iowa, was selected as Iowa's Guard Teen Panel (GTP) Representative, a role that serves as a voice for military youth while helping shape opportunities for connection, leadership, and resilience. In this position, Charlee represents Region 7, which includes Iowa, Missouri, Kansas, and Nebraska.

Leading with Purpose
As a GTP Representative, Charlee serves as a liaison between Guard youth and program leadership, helping communicate teen perspectives, share feedback, and support youth-focused initiatives at the state and regional level. The role requires initiative, collaboration, and a strong commitment to service — qualities Charlee has consistently demonstrated through her involvement with the State Teen Panel.

“I was challenged last summer in Omaha, Nebraska during the Region 7 Youth Symposium to step outside my comfort zone and consider how I could serve at a higher level,” Charlee said. “That experience helped me realize I wanted to use my voice to support other military teens across our region.”

Representing Youth Across Region 7
In this role, Charlee works alongside Child & Youth Program staff and teen leaders to support statewide events, promote youth engagement opportunities, and encourage other military-connected teens to step into leadership. Serving as the Region 7 representative also means helping ensure youth perspectives are considered when planning programs and activities that support Guard families across multiple states.

“Charlee brings thoughtfulness, maturity, and authenticity to this role,” said a CYP staff member. “That kind of leadership makes a real difference for military teens who are looking for connection, belonging, and a place to be heard.”

Looking Ahead
Charlee's selection as Iowa's GTP Representative reflects the continued emphasis on youth leadership within the Iowa National Guard community. By stepping into this role, she joins a legacy of teens who have helped strengthen connections between Guard families and create spaces where youth feel supported, empowered, and valued.

Opportunities like the Guard Teen Panel and GTP leadership roles are part of the Iowa National Guard Child & Youth Program's ongoing mission to foster resilience, build confidence, and develop capable young leaders among military-connected youth.

As Charlee begins this new chapter, one thing is clear: leadership doesn't start with a title — it starts with the willingness to serve.

Chain of Confidence: A Camper's Turnaround

It was Monday at camp when one of our youth sat off to the side, fighting back tears. He wanted to go home. Homesickness is common that first day — unsure, overwhelmed, and wondering if they belong.

I knew if we could just make it to Wednesday, things might look different. So I pulled out my old ring-and-chain trick and told him, “If you can figure out how to get the ring off, you can keep the chain.”

It took some time, but he didn’t give up. When he finally solved it, he earned that chain fair and square — and a big smile to go with it.

This photo was taken on Wednesday. The same camper who once wanted to leave now stood surrounded by new friends, proudly wearing his chain.

Moments like this are why our program matters. Sometimes all a kid needs is a small win, a little confidence, and someone who believes they can do it. That’s what we’re here for.

Legacy Rock Friendship

Behind the Picture | Summer Camp 2025

At first glance, it’s just two smiling girls and a painted rock. What you don’t see is the story behind the smiles.

Rylee and Isla met at summer camp — two strangers who quickly became inseparable friends. From campfire laughs to shared cabin moments, they built a bond that felt like it had always been there.

When campers were asked to paint a Legacy Rock to represent their week, Rylee didn’t hesitate. She painted herself and Isla. Her new friend wasn’t just part of the week — she was the highlight of it.

Though Isla is moving out of state soon, the two are already planning ways to stay in touch. Their rock may be small, but the memory it holds is lasting.

Behind the picture is a friendship that began at camp — and will continue far beyond it.

Fall Family Festival Strengthens Guard Family Connections

Camp Dodge – Johnston, Iowa | October 25, 2025

Published October 29, 2025

Military families came together at Camp Dodge for the annual Fall Family Festival — a day built around connection, resilience, and readiness. From the first welcome to the final goodbye, the installation felt like a reunion space for Guard-connected kids, parents, and caregivers.

State Teen Panel members set the tone the moment families arrived. They handled setup, greeted guests, and guided younger participants through each activity, showing what peer leadership and service look like in real time.

Partnerships with the USO, community organizations, and therapy-animal volunteers filled the schedule with meaningful moments: crafts, pumpkin painting, live demonstrations, and hands-on games that helped families relax and reconnect.

Why it matters

  • Connected families strengthen Soldier commitment and readiness.
  • Shared positive experiences lower stress and reinforce resilience over time.
  • Events like this advance the Iowa National Guard mission to prioritize People first.

Families said it best

“Programs like this help families feel supported.”
“These events support family well-being and ultimately improve retention.”
“It was made possible for us to connect and our kids to reconnect.”
“There was so much to do!”
